passage: Suraj, put that packet down a moment and listen. I'm Wasim, your grandfather, and I once believed a poster too. I was ten. A film wrestler on a biscuit tin said the biscuits made you strong like him, and I ate them for a month, flexing at the mirror. Nothing changed, except that my pocket money vanished. Finally I asked my father, "Does this really make me strong?" He laughed kindly and read the back of the tin with me. He said the poster was there to sell tins. "Ask before you believe," he told me. So ask your mother about that packet with the cartoon lion, beta. She may say yes, she may say no, but you will know more.

qa.q: How long did Wasim eat the biscuits?
qa.a: He ate them for a month.

qa.q: Why did ten-year-old Wasim keep eating the biscuits?
qa.a: He believed the wrestler on the tin when it said the biscuits made you strong.

qa.q: What could Suraj do about the packet with the cartoon lion?
qa.a: Ask Suraj's mother whether the snack is really good before believing the cartoon, as Wasim suggests.

qa.q: How did Wasim's father react when he asked if the biscuits made him strong?
qa.a: He laughed kindly and read the back of the tin with him, explaining that the poster was there to sell tins.

grounding: A child believes an ad's claim about a snack making him strong and learns to ask a parent whether it is true.
